newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian senator may quit after PM calls in police.
newsitem.headline: Australian senator may quit after PM calls in police.

text.p: A key Australian independent senator embroiled in an abuse of perks scandal said on Wednesday he was considering his political future, as a police probe began and pressure mounted to recall parliament over the affair.
Mal Colston, whose Senate vote has been vital to government reforms passing the upper house, said he would decide soon if he would relinquish the key post of Senate deputy president.
But the Labor opposition and minor Senate parties demanded he resign altogether and urged that the Senate be recalled to deal with him.

Prime Minister John Howard, under increasing fire over ethics in his year-old conservative government, announced on Tuesday that police would be asked to investigate allegations the senator had abused his parliamentary entitlements. Howard urged Colston to stand aside as Senate deputy president.
Colston, who defected from the Labor Party last year to sit as an independent, said in a television interview on Wednesday he would consider his position as deputy president.
"I will make a decision in relation to that between now and when the Senate resumes (on May 6)," said Colston, who has so far shown no signs of budging.
He added he had not received the "respect and support" he felt his senate colleagues owed him as deputy to the president, who runs the chamber.

Meanwhile Colston's son Doug, who also works for him, scuffled with journalists outside the family's Queensland home on Tuesday and a neighbour told reporters that Colston had flown to Vanuatu in the South Pacific.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley said Howard should pressure Colston to quit the Senate.

"What we would obviously hope to achieve is his resignation from parliament and his leaving of the position of deputy presidency which is something that should have occurred months ago," Beazley said.
Howard's administration does not have a majority in the Senate and has relied on the support of Colston and another independent to pass key reforms, including budget cuts.
If Colston, who denies breaking the law, is forced out he would be replaced by a Labor politician because he was a party member when elected, jeopardising future government reforms.

Howard's Liberal-National government, which pledged new ethical standards when it swept to power after 13 years in opposition, has been rocked by a widening scandal over allegations of abuse of parliamentary benefits.
The government said on Tuesday a lower house National Party backbencher and a recently-retired Liberal senator would be charged with fraud over travel claims. Both deny any wrongdoing.
And the government has been closely linked to Colston because of its support for his election as deputy president, which brings extra pay and benefits.
Political opponents, former staffers and at least one family member have charged Colston everything from the illegal to the comic in a saga that has dominated political coverage.

Among the accusations is that Colston held a chauffer-driven car outside a local supermarket until midnight to buy chicken at half price, asked the parliamentary library to do his son's university work and flew across the country and back to amass frequent flyer points.

Howard was forced to abandon the senator on Tuesday after a former Colston employee who had taken responsibility for 43 days of over-claimed travel allowances withdrew her statement and said Colston had always handled his own expenses.
